video_title: WNBA Stars Are Finally Getting PAID — But Will They Keep It?

quotes.speaker: Cassandra Negley
quotes.summary_phrase: WNBA players face financial challenges with sudden salary increases
quotes.excerpt: What happens when suddenly your annual salary is 1.2 million? Like, how do you treat that?
quotes.quote: Well first of all, thank you. I'm always really interested in the money aspect and one of the big questions I had was for a lot of players who made maybe around 150 to 200,000, specifically in the W we're talking. What happens when suddenly your annual salary is 1.2 million? Like, how do you treat that? What do you do? Suddenly you have so much money and we always have these stories of NFL players and NBA players going bankrupt or rookies just spending all their cash.

quotes.speaker: Cassandra Negley
quotes.summary_phrase: Financial advisors urge WNBA players to maintain their budgets
quotes.excerpt: they tell their clients all the time, like, live like you still live. Don't live outside of your means.
quotes.quote: And so his big thing, as well as Nikiya Sanford-Lawson, who I spoke with, a former WNBA player who's now a financial analyst, they tell their clients all the time, like, live like you still live. Don't live outside of your means. Like, follow the budget that you've had. Maybe you can splurge on something, but really be thinking about not necessarily spending all of that extra money. I spoke to some players who have bought cars because we all love cars and I'm all about it. I feel like a car is just you buy what represents you. But they also talked a lot about working with financial advisors, putting it into 401ks.

quotes.speaker: Cassandra Negley
quotes.summary_phrase: WNBA players make smart long-term investments and utilize benefits
quotes.excerpt: She has real estate holdings in Atlanta, near her hometown of Atlanta, because her financial agency had helped her do that.
quotes.quote: I had a one-on-one with Raven Johnson who told me that she, and this is before she was drafted to the Fever, she has real estate holdings in Atlanta, near her hometown of Atlanta, because her financial agency had helped her do that and it's a huge investment. Like, these players are spending their money in ways that is going to help them in the long run. The last thing I'll kind of say just to kick off this conversation is as much as it was about salaries, it was also about benefits. So your 401k, which is a 140% match, which is huge. Player programs, family planning that can cost a lot, and then retired players can also tap into some of these programs for the first time in this new CBA.

quotes.speaker: Caroline Fenton
quotes.summary_phrase: WNBA players' financial literacy and access to investment advice
quotes.excerpt: there are different tiers and levels of financial advising when you have money.

text_blocks.speaker: Caroline Fenton
text_blocks.text: There was one part of your article that really stood out to me. And this was a player who said, 'I have $10,000.' And like came to an investment account to invest. She's like, 'I have a comma in the amount of money that I have.' So like, 'I'm walking in, swaggy walking, I'm a rich girl.' And he's like, 'Yeah, no, no, no, you need at least five times that to even open an account here.' So I think that's another thing is the perspective of you might be coming out of college or you might be making now $150,000 when you were previously making $40,000. That's a massive leap maybe for you. And $150,000 is nothing to scoff at. That's a lot of money. But in the grand scheme of things, maybe in the grand scheme of the league and the grand scheme of being a professional athlete, that's pennies.

text_blocks.speaker: Cassandra Negley
text_blocks.text: I'm so glad that stuck out to you because that was Nikiya Sanford-Lawson was great to talk to. I laughed on the phone when she told me that because I also felt it. And she told me this whole story of she gets dressed up, she's going down the street in D.C. and she can tell when she walks in, they're kind of like, 'Oh, what are you doing here?' And the financial advisor has to tell her, 'Like, we can't work with you.' And that was complete news to me when Adewale told me that and the UBS guys kind of explained to me that there are different tiers and levels of financial advising when you have money. And there are certainly banks that will advise you if you have $50,000 in the bank. But there are advisors who will, as she experienced, will not work with you if you don't have that type of money. So as WNBA players are making more money in salary, they're also opening up more and more opportunities to have this type of higher investment help and really set them up for when the ball stops bouncing because as all of these people told me, including Jane P. Maranelli, who works at the WNBPA, like, you it does. It does no matter your name and you have to know what your money is going to do for you and what comes next afterward.

quotes.speaker: Caroline Fenton
quotes.summary_phrase: Athletes face pressure from family and friends after earning big money
quotes.excerpt: Money is nameless and faceless and genderless and raceless. When the money is there, people are going to come.

text_blocks.speaker: Caroline Fenton
text_blocks.text: And there was another part of your article and I don't want to give away everything, you have to go read it yourself. But Chemeka Holdsclaw said, 'I would say there's a majority of these young ladies who may be the first person in their family is making this type of money, and so they need someone to educate them on it.' That's another really difficult aspect of this is the family aspect, your friends aspect. I did radio for a long time with a former NFL player, in the league for 15 years, made a lot of money playing in the NFL. And he came from humble beginnings. And he said, 'All of a sudden, when the checks started to come in, when I started to play well, cousins, family friends, aunts and uncles, friends, just people that he hadn't talked to in a long time, coming out of the woodwork. Hey, can I have some money to pay my rent this month? Hey, can I have some money to pay my mortgage? Hey, can I have some money for, you know, whatever it might be?' And it might sound really innocent there, like, 'Hey, I promise I'll pay you back. Hey, it's only a little bit here and there.' But he said, 'I had to, whenever I made it big, that was the sacrifice that I had to make, cutting a lot of people out of my life because my only commitment is to my wife and my children.' Like, that is it. And if I give out money, if I pay these $10,000 loans here and there, which doesn't sound like a lot when you're making tens of millions of dollars, that really starts to add up. And then people still come by, 'Okay, again, I'll pay you back again. I'll pay you back again.' They keep coming back and asking for more money. So that's another unintended consequence of making more money is having to have really difficult conversations with people who may be looking at you with just big dollar signs in your eyes.

text_blocks.speaker: Cassandra Negley
text_blocks.text: I asked a few people about this specifically and I said, 'Like, do you notice a difference between men's athletes and women's athletes when it comes to that specifically?' And a lot of them, including Adewale, told me, 'You know, Cassandra, it's not about gender. It's about how much money you have.' And so as WNBA players are making more money, and we see this at the college level too, right? Like all of these players making big money in NIL. When I looked up numbers, Flau'jae's valuation, I think was like 1.5 million. You have people around you who want that money. You think of like when you win the lottery, like how many people suddenly come out of the woodwork or want to manipulate you or use you for money. That's just it's definitely an athlete problem, but it's also an issue whenever you have tons of cash.

text_blocks.speaker: Caroline Fenton
text_blocks.text: Yeah. Money is nameless and faceless and genderless and raceless. It's just, hey, when the money is there, people are going to come. And we've seen some brilliant businesswomen come out of the WNBA. Candace Parker, Sylvia Fowles. The list goes on and on of players that have continued to make money and build upon their brands. It's going to be fascinating to see in this iteration, in this generation of the WNBA. Look at Shaq. He's like the perfect example of, Shaq, Michael Jordan is another one, capitalizing on the Jordan brand, athletes that have been able to make even more money after they're done playing than they did when they were in the league and just making smart business decisions.
